sections.title: How does the Pizza baking calculator work?
sections.html:
The Pizza baking calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports pizza bottom temperature in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the baking surface and the dough's origin); then you type in the temperature, the pizza thickness, the dough density and the dough heat capacity.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Pizza baking calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

C=A × heating time + B × the square root of (heating time)
Pizza bottom temperature=-5000 × the square root of (PI) × B × the square root of (oven temperature conductivity) ÷ oven thermal conductivity + temperature
C1=(1 ÷ 1000) × dough heat capacity × dough density × pizza thickness × (boiling temperature of water − dough's temperature)
Α coefficient=C2 ÷ (latent heat × water density × pizza thickness)
C=C1 + C2
Oven v₂₁ coefficient=(-pizza bottom temperature + temperature) ÷ (pizza bottom temperature − dough's temperature)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Density, opening in grams per cubic centimeter
  • %, opening in percent
  • Time, opening in minutes / seconds
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Density, opening in grams per cubic centimeter

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Pizza baking calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Scaling a recipe up or down
  • Working out timing so everything finishes together
  • Checking portions before you shop
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the temperature, the pizza thickness and the dough density — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Pizza baking calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns pizza bottom temperature, derived from the temperature, the pizza thickness and the dough density. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Pizza baking calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the temperature, the pizza thickness, the dough density and the dough heat capacity, which is 11 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter temperature in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Temperature opens in Celsius and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Oven thermal conductivity = 0. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Pizza baking calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
